sections.heading: What does a migraine attack feel like?
sections.body:
The NHS describes migraine as a set of symptoms, not just a headache. These often include a throbbing headache on one side of the head, nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound. Other symptoms can include feeling very tired, craving certain foods, mood changes, a stiff neck and needing to pass urine more often.

Some people get an aura before the headache. An aura can involve sight problems such as zigzag lines or flashing lights, or pins-and-needles numbness. An aura appears gradually over a number of minutes and generally lasts less than an hour.

An attack can pass through several phases. Early warning symptoms can appear hours to a day or two before an attack. After the headache settles, lingering symptoms may last up to two days before a person feels healthy again. Not every phase occurs in every attack.

sections.heading: What types of migraine are there?
sections.body:
Migraine without aura is the most common form, making up about three quarters of cases in one review. Migraine with aura has several subtypes. Typical aura involves changes in vision, other sensory symptoms such as tingling, or problems with speaking. Brainstem aura includes at least two symptoms during an episode, such as vertigo, double vision, balance trouble or slurred speech.

Some people have aura symptoms but no headache, which is sometimes called silent migraine. Hemiplegic migraine is a rare type that involves temporary weakness or paralysis on one side of the body. It can run in families or occur without a family history. Vestibular migraine is migraine with dizziness, unsteadiness or vertigo, and is sometimes called migrainous vertigo. Chronic migraine means migraine headaches on at least 15 days of the month for more than three months, with or without aura.

sections.heading: How is migraine diagnosed?
sections.body:
NICE advises a headache diary, kept for a minimum of eight weeks, recording how often headaches happen, how long and how severe they are, other symptoms and all medicines taken. For migraine linked to periods, a diary covering at least the next two periods is advised.

A secondary headache is one caused by another problem. NICE says a GP may refer for tests or to a specialist if a secondary cause is suspected. Examples include a head injury within the past three months, headaches that start very suddenly, and problems with speech or balance that happen regularly and are getting worse. People with tension-type headache or migraine are not referred for imaging if they have no signs or symptoms of a secondary headache.

sections.heading: What treatments are there for migraine?
sections.body:
The NHS says migraine cannot be cured, but treatment can help manage attacks and prevent them. Options for attacks include painkillers such as ibuprofen and paracetamol, triptans, gepants and medicines for nausea. Gepants are a newer class, and a Scottish NHS pathway says the gepant rimegepant can be considered when triptans have failed or cannot be used. The Migraine Trust says gepants do not appear to cause medication overuse headache, while triptans and painkillers can.

The NHS lists preventive options including beta blockers, antidepressants and medicines for epilepsy. It also lists acupuncture, relaxation techniques, cognitive behavioural therapy and vitamin B2. A Scottish pathway also names candesartan, CGRP antibodies, flunarizine and botulinum toxin. In the UK, CGRP antibodies, gepants and flunarizine are generally prescribed by headache specialists rather than GPs.

Medication overuse headache is a pattern in which headaches keep coming back because of frequent use of pain medicines. The Migraine Trust says painkillers, ibuprofen, triptans and opioids can trigger it.

sections.heading: Living with migraine: what helps day to day?
sections.body:
The Migraine Trust says attacks usually result from several factors together rather than one trigger alone. It lists skipped meals, poor sleep and high stress as common contributors. The NHS says avoiding known triggers may reduce attacks, and that eating and sleeping well and regular exercise can also help.

Keeping a diary may help a person notice patterns, with entries such as sleep, meals, caffeine, alcohol, stress, weather and the menstrual cycle. The Trust cautions that cutting out foods or drinks believed to be triggers may not lead to fewer attacks. Regular bedtimes and wake times are recommended, since too little and too much sleep can each trigger attacks in some people.

Intense exercise can trigger attacks in some people, but regular exercise at a manageable level can be positive for most. Stress is a common trigger, and the Trust describes a let-down attack that happens when stress falls away.

sections.heading: When should someone get help for migraine?
sections.body: The NHS says to call 999 for a sudden, extremely painful headache, trouble speaking, loss of vision, confusion, a seizure, or weakness on one side of the body. Urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP the same day is advised if an attack has lasted longer than 72 hours, if an aura lasts longer than an hour, or if the person is pregnant or has just had a baby. A routine GP appointment is advised if headaches keep happening or are not controlled by treatment. The NHS says a GP may refer someone to a neurologist, a doctor who specialises in the brain and nerves, if the diagnosis is unclear or attacks are not controlled by current treatment. NICE says a clinician should consider medication overuse headache when headaches become more frequent or worse in someone who often takes pain medicines.

faqs.a: The NHS says migraine cannot be cured, but treatment can help manage attacks and prevent them. MedlinePlus likewise says there is no cure, but there are drug-based and non-drug ways to make living with migraine easier. Treatment for attacks includes painkillers, triptans, gepants and medicines for nausea. The clinician decides which treatments suit the individual.

faqs.q: Is migraine just a bad headache?
faqs.a: The NHS describes migraine as a set of symptoms that often includes a one-sided throbbing headache, nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound. Some people also have an aura, such as zigzag lines, flashing lights or pins-and-needles numbness. Others have tiredness, food cravings, mood changes or a stiff neck.

faqs.q: Can someone have an aura without a headache?
faqs.a: Yes. The Migraine Trust says some people have aura symptoms but do not get a headache afterwards. This is sometimes called silent migraine or migraine aura without headache. The NHS advises urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP the same day if an aura lasts longer than an hour.

faqs.q: Is a brain scan needed to diagnose migraine?
faqs.a: NICE says people with tension-type headache or migraine are not referred for imaging if they have no signs or symptoms of a secondary headache. Diagnosis relies on the pattern of attacks, and NICE advises a headache diary. A GP may refer for tests or to a specialist if a secondary cause is suspected.

Frequent use of pain medicines can lead to medication overuse headache, in which headaches keep coming back because of the medicine. The Migraine Trust says painkillers, ibuprofen, triptans and opioids can trigger it. NICE says a clinician should consider it when headaches become more frequent or worse in someone who often takes these medicines.
